The NASCAR Channel: How NASCAR Built a FAST Channel Worth Watching

AuthorSky Muller

Published
September 22, 2026

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 5:57
Instaread

We sat down with Dan Barker, Senior Managing Director of Content Strategy and Distribution at NASCAR. Dan has spent seven-plus years shaping how fans find and experience the sport. The centerpiece of that work the last few years has been launching the NASCAR Channel, the free ad-supported streaming television (FAST) channel that went live in January of 2025.

Here is how NASCAR built it, why they took their time, and the role the always-on L-Bar plays in keeping it feeling live and fresh.

Late on purpose

Most major sports had already planted their flag in the FAST space by the time NASCAR arrived. Dan does not shy away from that.

“We were almost so late that it worked to our advantage,” he said.

Being late had upside. NASCAR got to watch the market mature. They saw what other sports platforms were doing well and what they were not. And they walked in with a built-up appetite for NASCAR content that had nowhere to go yet.

Dan’s approach to the build was measure twice, cut once. That mindset showed up in every decision that followed.

The perfect content blend

A FAST channel is easy to spin up and easy to get wrong. The lazy version is a wall of archive footage that turns into a classic channel by default.

That is not what NASCAR wanted. The archive is the spine, and telling the story of the sport matters. But Dan built the channel on a blend: newsy programming, original content, and live racing.

The strategy runs on one principle. “It’s an act of fan service more than anything else,” Dan said. “The revenue is great, but it’s secondary to audience extension and fan service.”

That fan-first thinking shaped the hiring too. Dan brought in subject matter experts who live and breathe the sport, because people making content decisions need to think like the fans watching.

A smart, patient rollout

NASCAR launched exclusively with Tubi for a small window. The reasoning was sharp. Tubi was owned by FOX, and FOX had the Daytona 500, so the channel could ride the sport’s biggest moment for promotion.

From there it scaled fast. The NASCAR Channel is now on more than 10 distribution platforms, with Sony PlayStation among the most recent additions. Behind the scenes, the library has grown to over 3,000 assets managed through their tech partner Amagi.

To keep the schedule full and fresh, NASCAR leaned on partnerships. A Sirius XM tie-up turned the Morning Drive show into a video property and unlocked a daily live block. A five-year FloSports partnership feeds short track content that introduces fans to the next wave of drivers. And a new studio in Concord powers original programming like Memory Lane, where Hall of Fame drivers sit in a director’s chair and walk through their careers.

“The majority of them have burst into tears,” Dan said. “Which is awesome, because these are tough old dudes.”

The L-bar: always on, always fresh

Here is where Tagboard enters the story.

The NASCAR Channel runs a live L-bar, powered by Tagboard, that wraps the screen with real-time information. Point standings. Driver stats. Latest results. Promotional material. As the sport heads into its postseason chase, that live layer keeps fans up to date without ever leaving the stream.

For Dan, the L-bar does real work. “It keeps it up to date,” he said. “There’s a freshness and a timeliness to it that provides stickiness to the platform.”

It’s also flexible. During the channel’s Mark Martin tribute month, the team rebranded the L-bar in Martin’s most famous car scheme and dropped in a QR code so fans could buy his book right from the screen. That is the L-bar doing double duty: engagement value for the audience and revenue and promotional value for the business.

Dan was candid about the bar to clear. An always-on graphic can start to feel like background noise if you let it. The answer is to keep it relevant, keep it updated, and treat it as the front of the house.

“It’s the front of the house,” he said. “It looking good and sharp and polished is really important, because if you’re on the channel, we will leave it up.”

That is exactly the use case Tagboard is built to push on. A set-it-and-forget-it, always-on experience is newer ground for a lot of live graphics workflows, and NASCAR has helped stretch what is possible. Dan put it plainly: “We’ve stretched Tagboard’s capabilities a little bit, which is cool to see.”

More product updates are coming to support this kind of always-on workflow. Because Dan is right about where the value sits. When fans know real effort is going into what is on screen, the L-bar stops being decorative and starts being a reason to stay.

If you’re not winning, you’re losing

Ask Dan what makes a partnership work and he reaches for a line from the sport itself.

“If you’re not winning, you’re losing,” he said. “Working in racing, that’s a real thing, man.”

That is the mentality behind the whole build. It shows up in the patience to launch the NASCAR Channel right instead of fast. It shows up in a fan-first content strategy that treats revenue as secondary. And it shows up in the partnerships that make the channel go, the ones built on shared goals, honesty, and respect.

The live L-bar sits right inside that same standard. It is the front of the house, always on, and it only wins if it stays fresh and relevant each day. That is a high bar. It is also exactly the kind of always-on use case NASCAR and Tagboard are pushing forward together.

Not everything lands every time. Dan is the first to say so. But the NASCAR Channel is what it looks like when a team keeps its foot on the gas.

As Dan put it best: “We’re cooking now.”

Less hardware. More storytelling.
